/itineraryStops/0/description.source_en:
Door-to-door pickup at your hotel in central Busan, between **09:00 and 10:00**. Your exact time is confirmed by WhatsApp the evening before, once the driver has the day's hotel list and can order the run efficiently — guests on the Haeundae side are usually collected last, because the coach leaves the city heading northeast toward Gijang-gun for the first stop.

The supported area covers the central hotel clusters: **Seomyeon**, **Nampo-dong / Busan Station**, and **Haeundae / Marine City**. If your hotel sits outside that area, the guide names the nearest meeting point when the booking is confirmed.

Please wait in the lobby 5 minutes before your confirmed time. Transit from the last pickup to ⟦G0⟧ is about 30–40 minutes depending on traffic.

/itineraryStops/1/whyOnRoute.source_en: **The route's iconic opener — Busan's most-photographed temple in its quiet window.** The 10:20 arrival lands before the major tour-bus surge (typically from 11:00), so the 108-stair descent and the Haesu Gwaneum viewpoint are still walkable without queuing. Its Gijang cliff-top location also starts the day at the route's far northeast point, so everything after flows one-way down the coast — Cheongsapo next, then the capsule ride toward the city — with no backtracking.

/itineraryStops/1/description.source_en:
**⟦G0⟧ (해동 용궁사) — Korea's most famous seaside Buddhist temple** — perches on the rocky cliffs of Gijang-gun on Busan's northeastern coast, one of the very few major Korean temples NOT set in the mountains. Originally founded in **1376 during the Goryeo Dynasty by the great Buddhist teacher Naong Hyegeun (나옹 혜근, 1320-1376)** — a royal consultant and master who would help shape Korean Buddhism into the early Joseon era. 

Per legend, Naong was practicing asceticism at Bunhwangsa Temple in Gyeongju during a national drought; the East Sea god appeared to him in a dream and told him that building a temple on Bongrae Mountain (the original name of this seaside cliff) would restore the kingdom's prosperity. 

Naong founded the temple and named it **Bomunsa**, dedicated to Gwanseum-bosal (관세음보살, the Bodhisattva of Compassion). The temple was destroyed in the **Japanese Imjin Invasion of 1592** and lay in ruins for over 300 years until **Monk Ungang of ⟦G1⟧ began reconstruction in the early 1930s**. 

The current name, **⟦G0⟧ (Korean Dragon Palace Temple)**, dates only to **1974** — when Head Monk Jeong-am, during a 100-day prayer (jeong-geon kido), had a vision of the Goddess of Mercy descending on the back of a dragon, emanating multicolor light. 

The temple was renamed to honor this vision. The visit follows the temple's signature processional path: through the row of **12 Sibiji-shin (Twelve Zodiac Generals)** at the entry plaza, past the **7-story 'No-Accident Pagoda'** (where drivers leave coin offerings under a stone wheel-shrine), down the famous **108 stone stairs** (representing the 108 delusions of the Buddhist mind) through a small bamboo grove, and out onto the seaside terraces and Daeungjeon main hall. 

The **Haesu Gwaneum Daebul** (Sea-Goddess of Mercy statue) on the upper cliff is the most photographed view, framing both the temple rooftops and the East Sea. 

Hours **04:30-19:20 daily, last entry 18:50, FREE admission**. **Buddha's Birthday (May)** brings Yeondunhoe lantern festival displays.
